titre: The Supreme Court Invokes Liberty to Strike Down a Law on Bakers
accroche: In 1905, the U.S. Supreme Court strikes down a New York law that limited bakers' hours, in the name of freedom of contract.
contenu_vulgarise:
Utica, New York State, 1890s. An inspector finds that an employee of Joseph Lochner's bakery worked more than sixty hours in a single week. State law has forbidden this since 1895: the Bakeshop Act limits bakery work to ten hours a day and sixty hours a week, and also sets rules on sanitation, ventilation, washable floors, and a ban on household pets in the bakeroom, after years in which a share of New York's bakeries operated in poorly ventilated building basements. Lochner, already convicted once for the same offense, is tried again as a repeat offender, found guilty by the Oneida County court, and fined fifty dollars. He takes the case all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court, which hears arguments on February 23 and 24, 1905, and hands down its decision on April 17.

## A Liberty That Outweighs a Public Health Law

By a vote of five to four, the Court rules for him. Justice Rufus Peckham, who writes the majority opinion, frames the question this way: is the law a reasonable exercise of the State's police power, or an "unreasonable, unnecessary and arbitrary" interference with a person's liberty and with the right to make the labor contracts he thinks necessary to support his family? For the majority, nothing shows that baking is dangerous enough to justify such a limit: clean and wholesome bread does not depend on whether the baker works ten hours a day or sixty a week. According to the Court, the law is not a health measure, only an hours law disguised as a sanitary one, and so it interferes, without sufficient reason, with the freedom of contract protected by the Fourteenth Amendment.

Four justices dissent, in two separate opinions. Justice Harlan, joined by White and Day, answers that whether the baker's trade harms health had divided the judges of New York's own courts, which is enough to show that it is a matter of reasonable judgment and not a pretext, and that the Court therefore has no business substituting its view for the legislature's. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes goes further, in a separate dissent that becomes one of the most quoted in the Supreme Court's history: the case, he writes, "is decided upon an economic theory which a large part of the country does not entertain," and the Fourteenth Amendment, he adds, "does not enact Mr. Herbert Spencer's Social Statics," a reference to a work that preached the complete absence of state intervention in the economy. For Holmes, a constitution is not made to impose an economic doctrine, neither laissez-faire nor its opposite: it serves citizens of radically different convictions.

## Thirty Years in Which the Same Word Undoes Protection

Lochner does not remain an isolated ruling. It gives its name to an entire period of American jurisprudence, the Lochner era, during which the Court repeatedly invalidates federal or state laws that try to regulate minimum wages or working hours, in the name of the same freedom of contract. It takes until 1937 and West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish, which upholds a Washington State minimum wage law, for the Court to change doctrine. The history of social law thus does not move in a straight line toward ever more protection: the word "liberty" can just as well underpin the law that protects a worker as the ruling that undoes it.

carte.idee: In 1905, the U.S. Supreme Court strikes down a law limiting New York bakers to a sixty-hour week, in the name of freedom of contract. It then repeatedly invalidates minimum wage and working hours laws, until it changes doctrine in 1937.

quiz.question: Why do the four dissenting justices in Lochner v. New York (1905) disapprove of the majority's decision?
choix: Because they believe the bakers' law does not protect consumers enough against poorly baked bread
Because they consider that only a federal law, not a state law, can limit working hours
Because they judge that the Court substituted its own economic opinion for the legislature's judgment on a public health question
Because they think the law should also have applied to bakeries in hotels and restaurants
quiz.explication: Harlan, White, and Day consider that the link between hours and bakers' health is a matter of reasonable judgment the Court has no business setting aside. Holmes adds that the Constitution imposes no particular economic theory, and that a judge must not strike down a law passed by elected representatives simply because he finds it unwise.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Besides limiting working hours, what else did the 1895 Bakeshop Act regulate?
choix: The minimum wage of baking workers
Sanitary conditions in bakerooms, such as ventilation
The minimum hiring age in bakeries
The number of bakeries allowed per neighborhood
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1895 Bakeshop Act also set rules on sanitation, ventilation, washable floors, and a ban on household pets in the bakeroom, in addition to working hours.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which ruling ends the Lochner era in 1937?
choix: West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1937, West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish upholds a Washington State minimum wage law, ending thirty years of case law based on freedom of contract.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which work does Oliver Wendell Holmes refer to in his dissent to criticize the majority?
choix: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Holmes writes that the Fourteenth Amendment does not enact Herbert Spencer's Social Statics, a work preaching the absence of state intervention.
